passage: Jamal stood at the lockers in his school in Leeds, holding the new notice: students who missed two homework deadlines would lose the end-of-year trip. "That's not fair," he told Esther. "Dev looks after his little brothers every evening. He misses homework because of that, not laziness." Esther shrugged. "Rules are rules." "But why is it a rule?" Jamal said. "What's it for? To make us learn, or to punish?" He went quiet, then frowned. "Although if they make exceptions for everyone, the teachers can't run anything." He chewed his pen through maths, sketching arguments on the back of his notebook. By lunch he had drafted a short letter to the head of year asking for a way to explain missed work privately, instead of scrapping the rule entirely.

qa.q: What would students lose for missing two homework deadlines?
qa.a: They would lose the end-of-year trip.

qa.q: What does Jamal's frowning and chewing his pen suggest about what's going on inside him?
qa.a: He is genuinely torn: he feels the rule is unfair to Dev but also sees that teachers need some rules, so he is working out what he actually believes.

qa.q: Why was asking for a private way to explain missed work a sensible choice?
qa.a: It keeps the purpose of the rule while protecting students with real reasons, so it is more likely to be heard than a demand to scrap it.

qa.q: Why might Esther react differently to the notice than Jamal?
qa.a: She may see rules as simply there to follow, while Jamal is thinking about a friend's situation and what the rule is meant to achieve.

grounding: Shows a teen questioning a rule that seems arbitrary and weighing competing values to shape his own view of fairness.

passage: At the girls' hostel meeting, the warden repeated the rule: girls inside by seven, boys' block by nine. Vinita raised her hand. "Ma'am, why two different times? We have the same classes." A few seniors went still. The warden said it was for safety. "Then isn't the answer better lights near the gate, not locking us in?" Vinita asked. Her voice wobbled, but she kept going. Later, Dhruv from the boys' block messaged her: "Brave. But you'll get a black mark." She lay awake. Was she being disrespectful to someone who truly worried about them? Or was staying silent the real wrong? By morning she had decided: she'd keep asking, politely, and collect signatures for the lighting request instead of just complaining.

qa.q: What time did the rule say the girls had to be inside?
qa.a: The girls had to be inside by seven.

qa.q: Why was Vinita unsure she had done the right thing as she lay awake?
qa.a: She wondered whether questioning the warden was disrespectful to someone who cared about their safety, or whether keeping quiet about an unfair rule was the bigger wrong.

qa.q: What made Vinita's final plan a thoughtful one?
qa.a: She kept her challenge respectful and practical, asking for better lighting with signatures, which addresses safety instead of just attacking the rule.

qa.q: How does Dhruv see what Vinita did?
qa.a: He admires her courage but worries it will get her into trouble, so his message mixes praise and warning.

grounding: A teen in a hostel challenges a norm that seems arbitrary and works through the ethical tension to choose her stance.

passage:
Dear Tenzin,

Something happened and I need to think it through with someone who won't just give me a lecture.

In the chemistry test, I saw my friend Meghna copying from notes under her desk. You know her parents: if she fails, home becomes a war zone. Part of me thinks, who am I to report her? Another part thinks it isn't fair to everyone who studied till midnight, including me.

I used to believe cheating was simply wrong, full stop. Now I see it's tangled. Being loyal matters to me. So does honesty. They're pulling in opposite directions.

I think I'm going to talk to Meghna first, not the teacher. Tell her I saw, and that I won't cover for her if it happens again. Is that a cop-out?

Write back soon,
Reena

qa.q: What did Reena see Meghna doing during the chemistry test?
qa.a: She saw Meghna copying from notes under her desk.

qa.q: Why does Reena feel pulled in two directions?
qa.a: Reena feels torn between loyalty to Meghna, whose home life is hard, and honesty and fairness to the students who studied.

qa.q: What would you advise Reena about her plan?
qa.a: Talking to Meghna first is a fair step; she could also suggest Meghna seek help from a teacher so the pressure does not push her to cheat again.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He is likely to feel trusted, since Reena chose him because he won't lecture, and he may think carefully about how to answer her honest question.

grounding: A teen writes about a real ethical dilemma, wrestling with conflicting values to define her own moral stance.

passage: 'So, Bhavna, you asked when I started questioning stuff. Honestly? Class 11. Our school had this rule that the girls' section cleaned the labs after practicals while the boys went straight to games. Nobody asked why. I asked Sir once and he said, "Francis, it's always been like that." That answer bugged me for weeks. Like, is something right just because it's old? Then it got messier. My friend broke a beaker and a girl got blamed, and if I told the truth, he'd get the fine. I stayed quiet for two days and felt disgusting. On day three I told. He didn't talk to me for a month. I'd do it again, but I still don't think it was simple.'

qa.q: Who cleaned the labs after practicals under the old rule?
qa.a: The girls' section.

qa.q: How did Francis feel during the two days of staying quiet?
qa.a: Francis felt disgusted, torn between loyalty to a friend and fairness to the girl being blamed.

qa.q: What could Francis try to get the cleaning rule changed?
qa.a: Francis could raise it respectfully with the class teacher or student council, asking for a reason and suggesting a shared rota.

qa.q: How might the girl who was blamed see Francis's choice?
qa.a: She would likely feel grateful and relieved that someone told the truth for her.

grounding: Shows a teenager questioning a rule kept only by habit and struggling with a loyalty-versus-fairness dilemma.

passage: I'm Simran. My brother Jagdish is sixteen, and last Sunday he did something I'm still thinking about. When Kamla didi, who helps with the cooking, finished, Dadi handed her tea in the steel cup kept separately on the top shelf, like always. Jagdish took his own glass, poured tea into it, and handed that to Kamla didi instead. Nobody spoke. Dadi's face went stiff. Later I heard him on the balcony with Papa, asking, 'If we'd be hurt by this, why is it okay for her?' Papa didn't have an answer, only 'Dadi grew up differently.' Jagdish said, 'I know. I'm not angry at Dadi. I just can't do it anymore.' I don't know if he was scared. His hands were shaking a little when he poured.

qa.q: Where was the separate steel cup kept?
qa.a: On the top shelf.

qa.q: What might Jagdish's shaking hands suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he was nervous, knowing that breaking the family habit might upset Dadi, even though he felt sure it was wrong.

qa.q: How could Papa support both Jagdish and Dadi?
qa.a: He could talk with Dadi gently and privately, respecting her, while making clear the family can change the habit.

qa.q: What might this moment have been like for Kamla didi?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised, awkward or quietly respected, though Simran, telling it, can't know for sure.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager challenging an unfair household custom and defining his own sense of right, seen by his sibling.

passage: First week of term: the new rule said girls couldn't play football at recess, "for safety". Gurleen, fifteen, was furious but said nothing. Second week: she asked her friend Siddharth, "What's unsafe about us that isn't unsafe about you?" He didn't have an answer. She wrote down both sides, and some of her own arguments were weaker than she'd thought. Third week: she took a calm letter to the principal, signed by twenty girls and boys, asking for a trial week. The principal agreed. "It's not about football," Gurleen told Siddharth. "It's about rules having reasons."

qa.q: How many students signed the letter?
qa.a: Twenty girls and boys.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling in the first week?
qa.a: She was furious at a rule that seemed unfair, but not yet ready to act.

qa.q: What made Gurleen's challenge effective?
qa.a: She questioned the rule, tested her own arguments and then made a calm, reasoned request.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see Gurleen's question?
qa.a: It probably made him think, since he couldn't find a good answer.

grounding: Shows a teenager challenging an arbitrary rule and defining her own sense of fairness over three weeks.

passage: "Vikas, you ask why I never cared who sat where at weddings. When I, your Abhinav Dada, was sixteen, our village feast had separate rows for different families, as it always had. My friend Ramu, the potter's son, was put far away. I stood there with my plate, thinking: my father says all people are equal before God, so why these rows? If I sat with Ramu, my father would be shamed. If I didn't, I'd be a hypocrite. My hands were sweating. I walked over and sat beside Ramu. My father didn't speak to me for two days. Then, at the next feast, he came and sat with us too."

qa.q: Where did young Abhinav sit at the feast?
qa.a: Beside Ramu, the potter's son.

qa.q: What was young Abhinav feeling when his hands were sweating?
qa.a: He felt torn and afraid, caught between loyalty to his father and his own sense of right.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed the father?
qa.a: Abhinav choosing to sit beside Ramu, which later led his father to join them.

qa.q: How might Ramu have felt when Abhinav sat beside him?
qa.a: Surprised and respected, perhaps moved that his friend took the risk.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager he challenged an unfair custom and defined his own moral compass.

passage: Nazia, sixteen, and her cousin Zainab found a wallet on the way home from tuition: an ID card and two thousand rupees. Nazia's family had been short of money for months; her father's shop was barely running. Zainab whispered, "Nobody saw." Nazia felt the notes in her fingers. "Keeping it would help Abbu." "But it's someone else's Abbu's money." They argued all the way home. Nazia thought: if I lost this, I'd want it back. And if I keep it because I'm poorer, does that make it right? They took it to the address on the ID. A tired nurse opened the door and cried with relief.

qa.q: What was inside the wallet?
qa.a: An ID card and two thousand rupees.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling as she held the notes?
qa.a: She felt tempted and torn, knowing the money could help her family but that it wasn't theirs.

qa.q: What reasoning helped Nazia decide?
qa.a: Imagining losing it herself, and questioning whether being poorer made keeping it right.

qa.q: How might the nurse have felt opening the door?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, probably having feared the money was gone.

grounding: Shows a teenager wrestling with an ethical dilemma under money pressure and deciding by her own moral compass.

passage: At the Lucknow school, the rule was simple: girls had to stay inside the campus until 5 p.m. for "safety," boys could leave at 3:30. Yusuf, sixteen, had never thought about it. Then Parul, his project partner, missed their library session because she wasn't allowed out. "Why are boys safe at 3:30 and girls aren't?" she asked. Yusuf opened his mouth to defend it, then couldn't. That evening he kept turning it over. If the roads were unsafe, weren't they unsafe for everyone? Was keeping girls in actually protecting them, or just easier for the school? The next day, he and Parul drafted a letter to the principal suggesting the same time for all, plus a teacher on duty at the gate. His hands were sweating when he signed it.

qa.q: At what time could boys leave the campus?
What was Yusuf feeling as he signed the letter?
qa.a: He felt nervous, with sweating hands, but committed to what he now believed was fair.

qa.q: What did Yusuf and Parul suggest, and why is it a reasonable approach?
qa.a: The same leaving time for all plus a teacher at the gate; it addresses safety without treating girls differently.

qa.q: How might the principal see the letter?
qa.a: The principal may feel challenged or defensive, or may appreciate the students' respectful suggestion.

grounding: A teenager questions a school rule that treats girls and boys differently and works to change it.

passage:
"Nikita Didi, is it wrong to lie if it helps someone?"
"Depends. What happened?"
"Sana's parents think she was at my house on Saturday. She wasn't. She went to see a film with her cousin. Her mum called me and I said yes, she was here."
"Why?"
"Because Sana begged me. And her parents are really strict."
"How do you feel now?"
Gargi pulled her knees up. "Bad. But also like I was being a good friend?"
"Both can be true."
"But which one matters more? Honesty or loyalty?"
Nikita thought. "Maybe the question is: what would you want if you were her mum?"
Gargi was silent a long time. "I'd want the truth. I'll tell Sana I can't cover again."

qa.q: Where was Sana really on Saturday?
qa.a: At a film with her cousin.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel after lying to Sana's mum?
qa.a: Gargi felt guilty and torn, unsure whether being loyal made it right.

qa.q: What did Nikita's question help Gargi decide?
qa.a: To tell Sana she won't cover again, after imagining what she'd want as Sana's mum.

qa.q: How might Sana react when Gargi says she can't cover again?
qa.a: Sana might feel let down or annoyed at first, but may understand Gargi's reasons.

grounding: A teenager wrestles with the paradox of honesty versus loyalty after lying for a friend.

passage: I'm Farida. When I was fourteen, I noticed that in our building, Shanta Tai, who cleaned our flats, always took the stairs, all nine floors, even with buckets. I asked my mother why. "That's the rule," she said. "Lift is for residents." I couldn't stop thinking about it. It was the same lift and the same building. What made her different? I asked my friend Karthik, and he'd never noticed either. We went to the committee meeting together. My heart was pounding. I asked, "Who made this rule, and why?" Nobody had a good answer. It took three meetings, but the rule changed. Now when I see Shanta Tai in the lift, I feel something like pride, and also shame that I didn't ask sooner.

qa.q: How many floors did Shanta Tai climb?
qa.a: Nine floors.

qa.q: How did Farida feel after seeing Shanta Tai in the lift?
qa.a: Farida feels proud of changing the rule, but also ashamed of not asking sooner.

qa.q: What worked in how Farida challenged the rule?
qa.a: Asking plainly who made it and why, going with Karthik to the committee and persisting for three meetings.

qa.q: What is it like for Shanta Tai now, compared to before?
qa.a: She no longer has to climb nine floors with buckets, which is likely a real relief.

grounding: A person looks back on questioning a building rule that barred a cleaner from the lift, and getting it changed.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10-B
During the value education period, we discussed the school rule that girls must tie their hair in two plaits while boys have no hair rule. Aadhya asked why. I gave the usual answer about neatness.
Jatin then asked, "If it's about neatness, why doesn't it apply to boys with long hair?" The class laughed, but he wasn't joking. He listed three other rules he thought had no clear reason and one he thought was fair.
I noticed he was careful: he didn't call the rule stupid, he asked who it served. Some students looked uncomfortable; others nodded.
I didn't have a good answer. I told him so. I have asked the principal whether the student council can discuss the hair rule next month, and invited Jatin and Aadhya to present.

qa.q: What rule did the class discuss?
qa.a: That girls must tie their hair in two plaits while boys have no hair rule.

qa.q: What was Jatin likely feeling when the class laughed?
qa.a: He was probably serious and determined, maybe a little frustrated, since he kept going and listed other rules.

qa.q: What did the teacher do well after the discussion?
qa.a: The teacher admitted not having a good answer and asked the principal to let the student council discuss the rule, taking Jatin's questions seriously.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel about Jatin's questions?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel supported and encouraged, since her question was taken further by a classmate.

grounding: A teacher's note on a teen questioning a rule that seems arbitrary and testing it against fairness.

passage:
14 March
Today in debate practice we got the old question: would you steal medicine to save your sister if the shop refused to sell it? Nandini said yes, obviously, family first. I said yes too, then couldn't sleep.
Because if stealing is wrong, how can it also be right? And if it's right here, what else is "right" if I love someone enough?
Ammi says lying is always wrong. But last month she told the landlord we weren't home when we were. I didn't say anything. Was that wrong too?
I think I believe some rules protect people and some rules protect power. I want to be the person who can tell the difference. I don't know how yet.
Ask Nandini tomorrow what she really thinks, not debate-thinks.
Dilnaz

qa.q: What question came up in debate practice?
qa.a: Would you steal medicine to save your sister if the shop refused to sell it?

qa.q: How does Dilnaz feel after the debate practice?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels unsettled and conflicted, unable to sleep while wrestling with how stealing can be both wrong and right.

qa.q: What would you advise Dilnaz as a next step?
qa.a: Talk it through with Nandini and a trusted adult, as planned, and keep noticing which rules protect people.

qa.q: How might Ammi react if Dilnaz raised the landlord moment?
qa.a: Ammi might feel caught off guard or a little embarrassed, and it could open an honest talk about when rules bend.

grounding: A teen's diary wrestling with an ethical paradox and trying to form a personal moral compass.

passage: At the harvest feast in his grandparents' village near Thrissur, Jomon noticed it again: the men and boys ate first on the banana leaves, while his mother, aunts and cousin Harsha served, and ate cold rice afterwards in the kitchen. "Why?" he asked Appachan quietly. "It's always been like this," Appachan said. That wasn't a reason, Jomon thought. But making a scene would embarrass Ammachi, who had cooked since dawn. He sat still, torn, his rice going cold. Then he stood, took the serving pot from Harsha and said, "Sit. I'll serve this round." Harsha stared, then sat. An uncle frowned. Ammachi's mouth twitched, almost a smile.

qa.q: What did Appachan say when Jomon asked why?
qa.a: "It's always been like this."

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling as his rice went cold?
qa.a: He felt torn between his sense that the custom was unfair and his wish not to embarrass Ammachi.

qa.q: What choice did Jomon make, and why did it work?
qa.a: He changed the pattern through his own action, serving so Harsha could sit, which questioned the norm without a public argument.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel when Jomon takes the serving pot?
qa.a: Harsha is surprised, perhaps pleased and a little awkward at being asked to sit while the men watch.

grounding: Shows a teenager questioning a family custom that seems arbitrary and acting on his own sense of fairness.
